newsitem.title: LEBANON: Pope, feted in Lebanon, urges reconciliation.
newsitem.headline: Pope, feted in Lebanon, urges reconciliation.

text.p: Moslems and Christians gave Pope John Paul a rousing welcome to Lebanon on Saturday, on a visit he began with a veiled call for the withdrawal of foreign forces and an appeal to heal the wounds of civil war.

Crowds throwing rice and rose petals and waving flags, balloons and even tree branches greeted the Pontiff as he drove through Beirut on a 10-km (six-mile) route from the airport to the presidential palace on his first trip to the Middle East.

Tens of thousands of people lined the route taken by his bulletproof "Popemobile", in a welcome far more enthusiastic than he met a month ago on his pilgrimage of reconciliation to Sarajevo, the Bosnian capital.
In the first speech of his 32-hour visit, the 76-year-old Pope said he had come to Lebanon as a friend to encourage its sons and daughters, "so desirous of independence and freedom".
He said he had frequently alerted the international community "to help the Lebanese people to once again find peace in a national territory recognised and respected by all".
This appeared to be a veiled call for the departure of some 35,000 Syrian troops stationed in Lebanon and 2,000 Israeli troops who hold a border occupation zone in south Lebanon.

Many of Lebanon's Christian minority demand the departure of the Syrians and accuse the Beirut government of surrendering its powers of decision to Syria's leaders, while most Moslems see the departure of the Israelis as their top priority.
Billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri, a Sunni Moslem, said he and the Pope had raised the Israeli occupation during private talks at the presidential palace.
"I asked him to help Lebanon in implementing (U.N.) Resolution 425, which asks Israel to withdraw from Lebanese territory," Hariri said.
The Pope met separately with President Elias Hrawi, a Maronite Christian, as well as Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, a Shi'ite Moslem, and held talks with Moslem religious leaders.
Hrawi later presented the Pope, who will be 77 on May 18, with a surprise cake in the shape of the yellow-and-white papal flag as a presidential band played "Happy Birthday to You".
He hailed the Roman Catholic leader in a welcome speech as "the image of hope for all the Lebanese people".
Church bells rang across Lebanon and a 21-gun salute boomed as the Pope landed at Beirut airport, heavily guarded by troops backed by helicopters overhead and gunboats patrolling offshore.

The Pope said all Lebanese should be committed to peace and reconciliation and all should be given an equal opportunity to join in the future of the country that still bears the scars of a devastating civil war from 1975 to 1990.

"In this new Lebanon which you are slowly rebuilding, it is important to give a place to every citizen," he said, "particularly those who, inspired by legitimate patriotism, wish to become involved in political activity or economic life.
"From this point of view, the first condition for any truly democratic process is a just balance between the vital forces of the nation...," he added.

He was expected to return to the theme of co-existence later on Saturday at a meeting with more than 10,000 young Lebanese just north of Beirut at Harissa, the site of a huge modern hilltop basilica that looks out over the sea.
The Pope is known to regard Lebanon, the only Arab country that grants equality to all its people, Moslem and Christian alike, as an example in a region where Christian communities are in decline.

But many Lebanese Christians complain that they have been marginalised from politics since the civil war, while others refuse to participate because they believe the pro-Syrian government will not give them a fair deal.
The turnout for the Pope was big and enthusiastic in Christian districts with crowds lining the road several deep and packing balconies.
Many also turned out in Moslem districts, including Shi'ite women in full-length black chadors worn by fundamentalists. Many waved red-and-black Shi'ite flags and ululated as the Pope drove past.
"I believe he is here to talk about peace and this is why I came out to welcome him," said Faten Najdi, an 11-year-old girl. "It's true he's Christian, but he is for all the people."
